posts.post_text: We banned ChatGPT in our analytics department last month. Not because AI is bad — because nobody could explain where the numbers came from. When a regulator asks 'how did you arrive at this figure?' and the answer is 'GPT said so', you've got a compliance problem. The AI trust gap is real and growing.
posts.angle: High-scoring CRO post with three ICP prospects engaging — validate the auditability pain from a financial services angle, add the 'explainability isn't optional it's load-bearing' insight, no pitch needed
posts.draft_comment: The 'GPT said so' answer is genuinely career-ending in a regulated environment — that's not a fear of AI, that's just knowing how audits work. The trust problem isn't really about the output being wrong, it's that nobody can trace the reasoning back to a source anyone's willing to sign off on. Curious whether the ban came after a near-miss with a regulator or more of a 'we saw this coming' decision?

posts.post_text: We spent 18 months building a Power BI dashboard that our finance team refuses to use. They still export everything to Excel and email it around. The building part was easy. Getting people to actually trust the numbers enough to quote them in a board meeting? That's the real challenge nobody talks about. Anyone else hit this wall?
posts.angle: ICP prospect COO frustrated with BI adoption failure — validate the pain and reframe the real problem as trust, not tooling
posts.draft_comment: 18 months and it's the email chain that wins. Every time. The dirty secret is that dashboards don't fail because they're built wrong — they fail because nobody was ever sold on *why* the number in the tool is more trustworthy than the one Dave manually adjusted in his spreadsheet last Tuesday. Did anyone actually sit with the finance team and figure out where that trust broke down?

posts.post_text: Unpopular opinion: most operational dashboards are vanity projects. We had 47 KPIs on our ops dashboard. Nobody looked at it. Cut it to 5 metrics that actually drive decisions. Usage went from 10% to 85%. The problem with BI isn't the tools — it's that we measure everything and understand nothing.
posts.angle: ICP prospect (Director of Operations at Summit Group) engaging with a post about dashboard bloat — validate the 47-to-5 insight, add the 'why nobody looks' layer, no pitch
posts.draft_comment: The jump from 10% to 85% usage is the real stat here. Most teams build dashboards to prove they're measuring things, not to actually make calls faster — and there's a big difference. The honest question nobody asks before building is: what decision does this number change? Cut that filter on and half the metrics disappear before you even start.

posts.post_text: Hot take: self-service BI is a myth. We gave everyone Power BI licenses and what happened? 200 reports, zero consistency, three different definitions of 'revenue'. The promise of democratising data is great until you realise nobody agrees on what the data means. Build vs buy isn't the question — it's 'who owns the truth?'
posts.angle: Innovation Director at NorthStar Retail engaging on a post about BI chaos and ownership — validate the 'who owns truth' framing, add the insight that tooling is never the root problem, governance is
posts.draft_comment: The three definitions of revenue thing — that's not a Power BI problem, that's a 'nobody agreed before the tool arrived' problem. Giving everyone a licence just made the disagreement visible, which is actually useful. The real question isn't who owns the truth, it's who's allowed to *decide* what the truth is — and most orgs don't have an answer to that before they buy anything. Does yours?

posts.post_text: AI hallucinations in analytics are a security issue, not just an accuracy issue. If your AI tool generates a financial report with hallucinated numbers and someone makes a decision based on it, that's not a bug — it's a material risk. We need to start treating AI outputs with the same scrutiny as we treat user inputs.
posts.angle: CISO at a healthcare org is framing AI hallucinations as a security risk with a CEO prospect engaging — validate the framing, add the specific wrinkle about auditability that makes this harder than it looks
posts.draft_comment: The framing here is exactly right and I think it's still underappreciated. A hallucinated number in a report doesn't leave a trace the way a bad user input does — there's no log, no alert, no audit trail that says 'this figure came from nowhere.' That's what makes it nastier than a typical data quality problem. Who in your org actually owns that gap right now?

posts.post_text: Had a fascinating conversation with a client yesterday. They spent £200k on a BI platform and the only person who can use it is the one who built it. Self-service my arse. The gap between what vendors promise and what actually happens in a 50-person company is enormous. When will the industry admit that most BI tools are built for data teams, not business teams?
posts.angle: ICP prospect (COO at Sterling Consulting) engaging with a post about BI tools failing non-technical users — validate the pain with a sharp specific observation, add insight about where the real failure happens
posts.draft_comment: The £200k is almost never the problem — it's that the tool gets handed over and nobody thinks about the Tuesday afternoon when a sales manager needs an answer and the one person who built it is on holiday. Most BI implementations are actually just expensive dashboards with a self-service sticker on the box. The vendors aren't lying exactly, they're just demoing to the data team and selling to everyone else. How many of those £200k decisions had a non-technical person in the room when they picked the tool?

posts.post_text: Just had our quarterly review and the CFO asked why the numbers in our BI dashboard don't match the numbers in the ERP. Turns out three different teams were applying different filters to the same dataset. AI won't fix this. Culture will. But nobody wants to hear that.
posts.angle: Commercial Director at a likely mid-market industrial company exposing a data governance pain that's really a trust problem — validate the culture diagnosis and add the layer about what actually breaks first.
posts.draft_comment: Three teams, same dataset, three answers — that's not a filter problem, that's nobody agreeing on what the number is supposed to mean before they build anything. The AI conversation is a red herring here. Most dashboards fail not because the tech is wrong but because the business never decided who owns the definition. Who in your org is actually allowed to say 'this is the number'?

posts.post_text: Rolled out Copilot to 500 users last quarter. Usage after 90 days? 12%. The problem isn't the tool — it's that nobody knows what to ask it. We're essentially paying for a very expensive autocomplete. Shadow AI is the real story here — people are using ChatGPT on their phones because Copilot is too locked down.
posts.angle: IT Director surfacing a real adoption failure with enterprise AI — validate the shadow AI observation and reframe the root cause as a query literacy problem, not a tool problem
posts.draft_comment: The 12% number is brutal but honestly pretty normal — the shadow AI piece is the more interesting signal though. When people reach for ChatGPT on their phones instead of the approved tool, they're not being reckless, they're just trying to get an answer without needing a PhD in prompt engineering. The actual problem isn't lock-down or even training — it's that most tools make users do the translation work between 'what I need to know' and 'what I have to type'. Wonder if that's what your 88% are running into?
